text: The Common App allows you to submit up to 10 activities in the Activities section, ranked by importance to you. Colleges see them in the order you list them.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: The Common App requires you to self-report your grades in the Education section. Most schools will verify these against your official transcript after admission — misreporting is grounds for rescission.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: Common App school-specific questions, including the Why Us essay, appear under each school's tab in the Common App. They are separate from the main application and must be completed before that school's deadline.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: The Common Data Set for each school is published annually on their institutional research page and lists the exact factors they consider in admissions under section C7, including whether demonstrated interest is considered.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: MIT reinstated its SAT/ACT requirement starting with the class of 2028 and now requires scores from all applicants. Their admissions page states scores are used as a datapoint alongside the full application.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: The University of California system adopted a test-blind policy for all California applicants beginning with the class of 2025, meaning SAT and ACT scores are not considered in admissions decisions for CA residents regardless of whether scores are submitted.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: Georgetown requires SAT or ACT scores from all applicants and does not accept test-optional applications. This is documented on their undergraduate admissions requirements page.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: Yale's middle 50% SAT range for the class of 2027 was 1500-1570, per their published Common Data Set. Submitting a score below the 25th percentile does not automatically disqualify you but puts you below the typical admitted range.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: The University of California system guarantees transfer admission to a UC campus (though not necessarily your first choice) if you complete an Associate Degree for Transfer from a California community college with at least a 2.0 GPA in required courses. This is the ADT guarantee, documented on the UC admissions website.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: UC Berkeley publishes transfer admission data by major annually on their admissions website, including GPA ranges for admitted transfer students broken down by major.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: Many state university systems have articulation agreements with community colleges that guarantee specific course credits transfer. California uses ASSIST.org, which shows exactly which community college courses satisfy UC and CSU requirements.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: The National Merit Scholarship Selection Index cutoff varies by state and is published by NMSC after October PSAT scores are released each year. Students at or above their state cutoff are named Semifinalists; the cutoff for each state is listed on the NMSC website.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: Automatic merit scholarships at many state schools are tied to GPA and test score thresholds listed on the financial aid page — these are binding if you meet the criteria at time of admission, unlike discretionary scholarships.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: QuestBridge matches low-income high-achieving students with full four-year scholarships at partner colleges. The partner college list and scholarship terms are published on the QuestBridge website, and matched students pay nothing for tuition, room, and board.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: When deferred from a school in EA or ED, check the deferral letter or the school's admissions website to confirm whether they accept letters of continued interest — schools vary on this and some explicitly state that additional materials are not reviewed.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: Waitlist statistics including the number of students waitlisted, offered admission from the waitlist, and accepting from the waitlist are reported in each school's Common Data Set under section C2. Harvard admitted 0 students from the waitlist in 2023.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: AP scores of 4 or 5 earn credit at most selective schools, but the specific courses and credit amounts vary significantly by school and department. Each school publishes an AP credit chart on their registrar or admissions page.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: FERPA gives enrolled students the right to review their own educational records, including letters of recommendation, unless they waived that right when applying. Most Common App schools ask applicants to waive this right voluntarily.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: IB diploma holders receive credit recognition at most US universities, but the threshold varies — some schools grant credit only for Higher Level scores of 5 or above, others start at 4. Check the specific school's IB credit policy page.
label: evidence_based_advice

text: The CSS Profile institutional methodology counts home equity as an asset, while FAFSA federal methodology does not. Schools that use only FAFSA will not count your family's home equity in your Expected Family Contribution.
